subject: stainedGlassPeacock
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: peacock with fanned tail.
Style: stained glass with lead came.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a stained-glass peacock design with a fanned tail, using jewel-toned cell patterns with dark lead came lines separating the glowing panes to capture that lead-light aesthetic.

Now I'm sketching the overall proportions and pose: a standing bird roughly a meter tall with its tail fan rising behind it as a glowing semicircle disc about 0.85m in radius, and starting to lay out the skeleton — hips, spine chain up through chest, neck, head, plus leg joints reaching down to the feet.

I'm planning the head details, the S-curved neck, folded wings, and the layered tail structure (fan feathers plus shorter stiff underlying ones), then setting up a stained-glass color palette — a dark lead line color and a set of jewel-tone glass hues for the body panels.

For texture resolution, I'm calculating that a 2048px paint sheet gives sharp enough lead lines (~7mm) across the roughly 1.5m² painted surface, and considering adding subtle shading within the flat glass cells to keep that luminous stained-glass look rather than fully flat color.

Writing the glass paint function...

I'm confirming mix, noise, paint, resolve, rgb, and smoothstep are exported from the SDK, while warp isn't, so I'll skip it. For lighting I'll add a subtle top-warm tint based on the normal's y-component, and decide to keep the body painted solid while giving the tail feathers a glowing card treatment to evoke stained-glass windows.

Eye-spots and crest tips should also glow with flat gem tones, and each feather card will be drawn as a leaded stained-glass design: a vertical shaft with dark lead lines, alternating green/teal/gold panes along the barbs, and a concentric eye motif at the top running from gold outer ring through teal, deep blue, to a ruby-violet center with a highlight, sized to scale cleanly at 256px.

Now I'm working out the fan arrangement, placing each feather card along its own frame so the card plane holds both the radial axis and the tangential width direction, with the card facing along the flattened flow direction since the cards are double-sided and visibility from any face works.

For the glow, I'm leaning toward an emissive strength around 0.9 rather than full 1.0 to avoid oversaturating the stained-glass luminous effect once diffuse lighting stacks on top. I'm planning several layers of feathers, aiming for roughly 31 feathers in the main fan for density.

Spanning about 180-200 degrees, I'll add overlapping layers — a second, slightly shorter layer offset and leaning differently — plus two alternating eye-feather textures with different jewel palettes, and a shorter plain fringe layer underneath in golden-green without eyes. Working through the sizing math, with card width 0.2 and length 0.85, around 33 feathers at that radius gives enough spacing overlap (roughly 2.5x) to look dense rather than sparse.

Since the cards are all coplanar, I realize I need to stagger them in z to avoid z-fighting where they overlap — I'll give each layer a small z offset and alternate by feather index so neighboring cards sit on distinct parallel planes. I'm also considering a subtle forward lean or cup-shaped curve to the fan, tilting the tips slightly toward the flow direction for a more natural concave shape.

Now I'm thinking about root placement — having each feather's base spread slightly in x rather than all converging to one exact point, so the bundle reads as a believable cluster rather than a single pivot.

For the tail skeleton, I'm setting up a chain (tail1 through tail3) behind the hips, then attaching the fan feather group to the tail3 bone as a rigid parent. I'm structuring this as a ring of joints around a line perpendicular to the tail's axis, using a fan role so the feathers spread radially from that attachment point, with angle zero oriented toward world-up.

I'm working out the angular spread for the fan, roughly ±100° from vertical to mimic a peacock's fanned display, while checking the geometry so the feather tips (around 1.5m up, given a 0.6m tail base and 0.9m feather length) don't clip through the body or extend unrealistically far to the sides.

Now I'm figuring out how the tail joints ring around the spine, each offset slightly outward along its own radial direction, and reasoning through how to orient each item's local frame so its forward axis tilts toward the line direction while placing it at the right radius without accidentally mixing up world versus local Z offsets.

Given the risk of API mismatch with moved/frame directions, I decide the safer approach is to create separate rings for each feather layer, each with its own base frame positioned at a different z-offset along the spine, rather than trying to offset a single ring's items individually -- joint count should stay well within limits either way.

Actually same-plane feathers within a ring would overlap and z-fight against each other, so I need to split into multiple rings of fewer feathers each, offsetting z per ring so neighbors don't clash.

Thinking through the joint setup, I decide to give each of the three fan rings its own 4 joints, nested under the parent tail joint, so 12 joints total rather than complicating the rig further. Then I plan to draw the cards using the ring items returned from the ring builder, feeding them into the card renderer with the texture.

I'm setting card parameters like size, flow direction, lean, variation, and sink, plus texture selection logic that picks randomly between two feather textures per card using the rng option. I'm also thinking through how the ring's angle range should be divided across rings so items land correctly with inclusive endpoints, adjusting the spacing formula per ring index.

Each ring takes an interleaved subset of 33 total positions spaced by 6.25 degrees, with 11 items per ring spaced three steps apart, and the rotation direction is symmetric so sign doesn't matter. I'm placing the eye near the tip of the feather around 78% of its length, and adjusting the card's aspect ratio and viewBox dimensions to roughly match the feather's width-to-length proportions before writing the actual feather SVG.

Writing SVG code...

Adding feather barbs and a nested peacock-eye pattern of concentric ellipses...

Still shaping the vane outline...

Drawing the chevron bands...

Now I'm planning the body construction with stained-glass coloring: iridescent blue neck and breast, green back, barred brown wings, and a white face patch, using a spine chain to position the teardrop-shaped body between tail, chest, and head coordinates.

I'm laying out the skeleton as a single continuous chain running from rump through hips, mid-body, chest, and up through the neck segments to the head, with the root joint at the hips.

For head, I'll add it as a joint referencing a point on the neck chain with a forward-ish direction, following the same pattern as the example. Then I'm planning the tail chain, running backward from hips through a few points behind the body.

Now I'm thinking about building the body itself as a swept shape along the spine path from rump to chest, deciding between a loft or sweep approach with varying radius.

I'm reconsidering the rig structure—maybe the root hips joint should sit at the rump start, with legs instead hanging from a later spine joint at hip level, so the body sweep and pelvis placement stay consistent.

To avoid a zero-length bone between hips and spine1, I'm considering naming the hips as the chain's own root joint rather than a separate parent, since an unparented chain likely becomes the root automatically. I'll define hips with an aim direction, then let the spine chain continue from the next point onward while still keeping the body sweep bones referencing hips correctly.

Actually, maybe simpler to let the spine chain's path start directly at the hips position with a zero-length first segment — slightly risky since the bone direction between hips and the first spine joint could be undefined, but with no explicit aim it should just inherit the parent's orientation, so it's probably harmless for this case.

Actually maybe one continuous sweep works better: a single path running hips to chest to neck to head, with the bone chain spanning all three joints, letting the radius taper from body-wide to neck-thin for a seamless curve. That avoids separate cap-overlap issues between body and neck entirely.

I'm now plotting out the actual path coordinates, mapping how hip, chest, and neck positions connect with specific y/z offsets to get the right S-curve silhouette.

Working out the radius profile along that path, keying tube thickness at different arc-length points so it tapers appropriately from body to neck.

I'm also planning the glass paint scheme by region: blue for the neck/breast area, green along the back, with separate coloring for the belly based on position and normal direction.

Writing cell palette function...

I'll simplify by zoning purely off the pane's center y-coordinate relative to the body's centerline, roughly separating neck, chest, back, and belly/flank regions and assigning each a color family—blues for neck/chest, emerald/gold for back, deep indigo/teal for belly.

Defining color palettes...

Still tuning lead highlight blending...

Now thinking about the head: a small blue-teal glass sphere with smaller stained-glass cells, plus a decal for the face featuring white crescent eye panes with lead lines, applied onto the head part.

I'm working out the geometry for placing the eye decal on both sides of the head, computing the correct orientation vectors so the eye pattern faces outward correctly when viewed from the side.

Still drawing the eye details and crescent patch, then thinking through the crest design—thin curved shafts with teardrop tips scattered around the crown, possibly using a ring arrangement of feather hits near the top of the head.

Computing tip and control points via offsets along the item's facing axis...

I'll use `cross: true` for the crest tips so the cards form a right-angle pair readable from any viewing side, keeping it simple with 11 cards per count rather than a sphere tip. For the crest tuft texture I'm sketching a teal teardrop shape with a lead outline and a bit of glow.

Now for the beak, I'm planning upper and lower jaw pieces as short pointed sweeps in a pale amber horn color, with a joint attaching at the head.

Setting up the head's aim direction...

Confirming the local-space helper accepts mixed forward/up/left keys, then I'm sketching the head's proportions: neck radius around 0.03, head sphere slightly larger at 0.045-0.055 for a characterful look, beak length about 0.06, and eye decal sizing roughly 0.075x0.05.

Now I'm defining the beak as a tapered spike from base to tip near the head, keeping it simple with a circular cross-section so it reads as a round peacock beak.

I'm setting up the jaw joint attached to the head, defining a smaller lower beak sweep, and giving it a tan horn color. Then I move to adding eye decals onto the skull sphere.

For legs, I'm planning a digitigrade peacock-style structure with hidden thighs and long gray-brown tarsus segments, including forward toes and a hind toe, positioning the hip and foot joints and sketching the limb segment lengths for the IK chain.

Naming the chain joints hip, knee, ankle, and foot as the tip for each leg, with side-based naming for left/right. I'm thinking through the radius profile for the leg sweep—thick near the thigh tapering to thin at the tarsus—and settling on a glassy gray-amber color for the legs.

For feet, I'm planning three forward toes plus one back toe as small rods extending from the foot tip point at set angles, each tapering with a tiny claw spike, bound to the foot joint.

Checking the toe height placement so rod radius keeps the bottom resting at floor level, then tracing the leg attachment from hip at x≈±0.07 down through the chain to the tip joint, verifying the hip sits inside the body above its bottom edge for proper limb reach.

Comparing segment lengths against target distances: picking limb lengths of 0.15, 0.13, 0.19 gives enough slack over the straight-line reach so the leg bends naturally rather than locking straight.

Now I'm working out the wings — folded against the body sides with a brown-barred pattern and scapular feathers, planning to build them as an extruded teardrop profile in the side plane positioned near the body's widest point around x=±0.135.

I'm defining the outline points for the teardrop wing shape, then checking whether this thickness at that position would overlap the body's curved flank, deciding I need to push the wing slightly outward to x=0.15 to avoid burying it inside the torso.

Thinking through alternatives for how the wing should attach to the body's narrower rear section, considering sweeping the wing along the body's surface curve rather than placing it as a flat offset shape.

Instead of precise station mapping, maybe I should flatten the wing into stacked, overlapping feather cards arranged like scales across the body flank, each with a stained-glass brown-gold bar texture, leaning steeply along the surface in rows by angle and column by position — that would read as a convincing peacock wing.

To avoid z-fighting between overlapping flat-lying cards, I'll offset each row's lift so rear feathers overlay earlier ones shingle-style, matching how real feathers layer toward the tail.

For the wing design, I'm mapping deg values across each flank for feather rows, confirming that +X side corresponds to -90 degrees on the tube since 0 is up and rotation goes clockwise, with sign flipped depending on which side. The wing feather cards flow backward along z, similar to the body cards but with a shallower downward tilt.

For the body shape itself, I'm defining a function to get path parameter t for a given point, using the body path's closest-t lookup so the wing placement stays robust rather than relying on raw arc-length guesses. I'm figuring out the t range for the shoulder-to-rump region to loop through wing rows and columns, settling on roughly 4 rows by 8 columns per side for the feather card count, doubled for both wings.

I'm also planning the mantle scale cards for the green back, deciding to skip dense rump coverts but add a ring of short covert cards around the tail base to hide the root feathers, then considering whether a decorative chest cabochon fits the stained-glass aesthetic.

I'm skipping the glowing chest gem and eye glow, deciding instead to apply glow only to the feather cards, crest tips, and beak using the cards-returning meshes. I'm also weighing whether to add lead came detailing along the fan edges or a radial lead framework between feathers, though without a pedestal or ground element it may not be necessary.

I'm thinking through how to anchor the fan's feather shafts at the base, hidden beneath coverts and rump, using a small sphere-shaped lump as the tail root.

Now I'm setting up the ring geometry parameters, defining the fan's radial arrangement of feather roots around a frame axis parented to the tail joint. Writing ring config...

Thinking through the stacked z-offsets between fan rings (A through supports E), checking whether the small 0.015 increments are enough to avoid depth z-fighting given typical camera near/far settings.

I'm settling on 0.02 spacing with rings A,B,C at -0.38,-0.40,-0.42, and confirming the 6° lean applies equal forward displacement to all tips since the lean direction is perpendicular to the axis, so the planes stay parallel without intersecting — same logic holds for fringe layer D behind at -0.45.

Random size variation won't affect the plane itself, but spin rotation about the facing axis would tilt card planes about the radial axis, causing intersections near the axis — so I'll keep spin at 0. Now I'm checking feather density: with 33 main eyed feathers across the 200° fan, arc spacing near the eye position overlaps significantly with neighboring layers, meaning eyes get partially covered by cards in front.

To fix the hidden-eye problem, I should stagger feather lengths and eye positions across rings A, B, C so their eye ellipses don't directly overlap, adjusting the radial and lateral offsets between rings.

Now I'm planning out the full texture set: FEATHER_A and FEATHER_B for the eyed feathers, FRINGE for the gold/green chevron panes, SUPPORT and WING_FEATHER for the structural pieces, plus CREST_TIP and EYE decals — roughly seven textures total, which feels right for the complexity target. I'm debating whether the wing cards should glow like the tail or stay lit normally, leaning toward giving some glow to keep the backlit-glass effect consistent.

Writing the stained-glass paint helper and lead-line color constants...

Still writing color blending logic...

Checking whether paintSize 1024 gives enough resolution for the painted area (~1 m²), which works out to roughly 1.2mm per texel — plenty for the lead gap of ~6mm to render cleanly across a few texels.

Now I'm defining color palettes for different zones (blues, teals, greens, golds, indigo) and writing a zone-assignment function that picks a palette based on a point's position coordinates on the body.

Still refining body region thresholds...

Now I'm defining the body curve with a series of control points from hip to shoulder, using a catmull-rom spline, and figuring out which segment of that path corresponds to the spine joint chain for the skeleton.

Continuing the skeleton setup, I'm wiring the hips to aim at the first spine joint, then slicing the body path into spine (3 joints) and neck (3 joints) chains with parent relationships, and placing the head joint at the top of the path.

For the actual body mesh, I'm sweeping the body path with varying radius along the hips-spine-neck bone chain, using a low facet count without smoothing to get that faceted, low-poly glass look consistent with the rest of the style.

I'm defining a keyed radius function that interpolates between control points along the path, using normalized path positions and smoothstep easing to blend between the radius values at each keyframe.

Now I'm working out where the legs attach relative to the hips and body tube, checking that the hip position stays inside the body radius, then turning to how the wing cards attach to the body tube using the sweep function to find the right angle and lift at each t-value range.

Laying out the wing covert grid: columns running backward along t from shoulder to rump, rows spanning degrees from the upper back down to the flank, forming a 5x9 grid of cards per side, with larger cards toward the bottom edge and a backward lean for the flow texture.

I'm working out the flow direction and mirroring for the cards, deciding both sides can share one call since the wing texture is symmetric. For the feather texture itself, I'm sketching a rounded-tip feather shape within a tall rectangular viewBox, oriented so the tip points toward the downstream/backward flow direction, with a scalloped U-shaped outline and an outer bronze band.

I'm detailing the feather's chevron-patterned interior bands—bronze at the tip, then gold, then green, with V-shaped lead lines and a central shaft. Now I'm considering the peacock's hidden support feathers behind the main fan, thinking through their angle, size, and brown coloring so they peek out realistically between the fan feathers.

I'm also adjusting the layering of the rings—support, fringe, covert, and the main A/B/C bands—along the z-axis so there's no visible gap between the tail base and the body rump, nudging each depth value until the fan sits flush against the body cap.

Now I'm setting the fan base height above the rump, since the train should rise from the hips rather than sit level with it, then building a short tail joint chain from the hips outward to anchor the rings and adding a small quill-like sweep at the base for a tapered brown accent. I'm also checking the fan ring angles relative to vertical to make sure the feathers splay slightly downward rather than straight out, which should keep the overall silhouette natural.

I confirm the fan's span and height work with the default front-facing camera view, so the breast reads clearly in front of the spread tail. Then I move to designing crest shafts: setting up a radial arrangement near the crown with a partial angular range so the feathers form an upward-leaning cone rather than a full circle, giving each shaft a steep tilt and a slight outward curve toward its tip.

Now I'm working through the crest tips -- defining tip-facing card frames oriented along the direction from control point to tip, texturing them with a teardrop-shaped teal/blue design, and sorting out the Vector3 typing so offsets can be mutated directly. Then I start writing a reusable function for generating fan layers...

Still writing fan generation logic...

Item axis likely defaults tilt to 0, and partial angular ranges should place items correctly at both ends. Now I need to work out the ring angle lists for each layer, parameterizing counts per layer.

For the fan layers A, B, C with differing depth offsets and lengths, I'm computing each feather's angular range so indices map evenly across the -100° to +100° span, verifying endpoints land exactly at ±100°. The varying lengths across layers (A longest, B and C shorter) create a silhouette where A's tips peek out between the shorter B/C feathers.

To fix the jagged star-like outline this produces, I'm tightening the lengths closer together (A .86, B .84, C .82) and instead varying the eye position per layer — using three distinct feather textures with eye heights at different y-positions (46, 62, 78) so each layer's eyespot sits at a different radius, staggered roughly 0.067 apart plus a lateral offset, giving separated eye ellipses instead of a jagged edge.

Checking the math, the eye ellipses at those offsets still overlap slightly, so I work out the minimum separation needed to avoid that — roughly 35 units of vertical offset between eyes — meaning positions like 40, 75, and 110 would work better, though at y=110 the vane narrows enough that the eye ellipse barely fits. I'll just accept some partial overlap since front layers naturally occlude the back ones anyway.

Writing feather SVG generator function...

Building nested eye layers for the feather...

Planning the draw order: bands, barb leads, eye, then shaft (passing behind the eye), with the outline drawn last. I'm working out the vane's path geometry with curves tapering toward the tip and base, and setting up a few color palettes like emerald and teal-gold variants for the feathers.

Still finalizing color palettes...

Now I'm sketching the eye decal for the head, laying out brow stripe, cheek crescent, and eye circle shapes in the SVG viewBox.

Defining the white panes within lead divisions, placing the eye ellipse with amber iris, dark pupil, and small highlight, then adding dividing lines through the crescent to texture the glass as blue stained decals.

Working through the orientation math confirms beak placement mirrors correctly between the two sides of the bird depending on viewer direction, and the decal projection direction for the eye uses the signed axis to map onto the sphere.

I'm setting up the head geometry as a scaled sphere with proper bone attachment, applying a blue glass palette for head painting, confirming decal targets reference the correct Part object, and assigning flat or glass-paletted colors for the beak and leg surfaces.

For the legs I'm defining a grayish-tan palette and adjusting lead-line thickness and spacing for proportion, then thinking through flat colors for toes and claws, and considering whether to add a dark leading ring at the neck base to mimic stained-glass seams where color regions meet.

I'm also planning to add a couple more lead rings at the neck joints using surface loop cuts, being careful about the joint direction and risk of plane-cut errors, and considering wrapping these decorative additions in a try/catch so a failure there doesn't break the whole build.

On part count, I'm noting the wings alone could use around 90 cards per texture bundled into a single mesh, keeping total mesh count relatively low—maybe 60 meshes—while the target is somewhere between 180 and 340 parts, so I may need to add more discrete pieces to hit that range since parts themselves are cheap to create.

I'm thinking I could add crest shafts as sweeps, toes as rods and claws, and fan joints to push the model toward 100 parts, then go further by giving each feather its own visible quill as a thin lead-colored tube extending from the base, mimicking the bare quill look of a real peacock feather—generating dozens more parts this way.

Beyond the quills, I'm considering adding tiny stained-glass scale cards scattered across the neck as hackle feathers, though I need to figure out how to scatter them properly since the neck is part of the body's continuous sweep rather than a distinct surface.

I want the neck feathers flowing downward along the surface, tips pointing downstream, so I'll flatten the flow vector onto the plane with a slight backward tilt. For the scale texture itself, a small rounded shield shape divided into three panes with lead lines and teal/blue gradient panes works well, and I can reuse this same scale card for the breast region by extending the filter to include a lower z and y range.

I'm restricting the scatter to the front of the body (excluding head and back), using a breast scatter count around 140 with a minimum spacing, and keeping the card geometry simple at four triangles each. I'll grab a seeded random function for consistent placement, make sure the beak/jaw joint uses the correct bone reference, and skip adding extra geometry for the shoulder area for now.

I'm checking that the feet and toes rest exactly at floor level with nothing sinking below the surface, and verifying the overall model height stays reasonable with the fan and crest proportions I calculated. I also need to confirm the limb helper's reach from root to target foot position works correctly given the segment lengths and bend parameters.

For the toe attachment, I'm figuring out which joint in the leg chain represents the tip, confirming the last joint in the chain is the correct attachment point. Then I'm setting up the sweep function to generate the leg's visible geometry with a radius that tapers along its length.

Writing taper and toe placement...

Toes can stay rigid on the foot joint rather than forming their own chain, keeping things simple. Since wings are folded and skeletons should separate limbs properly, I should add shoulder joints for the wings — a `wingL` and `wingR` joint parented to the spine, positioned at the shoulder with a "wing" role, so the wing cards can ride on those joints.

I'll build a short wing chain per side (shoulder, elbow, wrist points along the flank) so the cards rigidly follow the correct bone rather than defaulting to the spine.

For types, I'll avoid importing the SDK's `Rgb` type and just define my own local RGB tuple type instead, keeping the zone function signature simple and self-contained.

Now I'm writing the glass paint function, blending cell colors with a glow tint near cell centers and modulating lightness with noise for texture...

I'm also working out TypeScript typing for the RGB tuple return value, making sure the array literal matches the expected readonly tuple type.

Now I'm starting the full build function, setting up the peacock's metadata and joints for the body structure.

Still defining joint hierarchy...

Finishing the wing chain definitions and naming shoulder/elbow/wrist joints, then setting up leg chains parented to the spine. Now I'm computing path parameters for shoulder and rump positions to lay out wing card geometry across the body sweep.

Working out row angles, lift offsets, and card sizing to place feather-like cards along each wing frame, varying size slightly by row and alternating textures between a bronze-gold-green palette and a blue-teal palette for visual variety.

Now I'm drafting the SVG path strings for the feather vane shape itself, defining the lead color constant and a curved outline that tapers from the quill tip down the length of the feather...

Writing feather texture bands...

Still drawing eye layers...

Settling on eye ellipse widths (14x20 gold, narrowing inward for rings/core/pupil) and checking eye spacing doesn't overlap too much by comparing normalized distances against the ellipse radii.

Writing wing feather texture function...

Still writing shield paths...

Now I'm setting up the head crest ring using a circular placement function around the crown point, with 9 evenly spaced segments tilted to lean outward along the surface normal.

Writing crest shaft geometry...

Checking a few more API details — offset accepting a direction input, the sweep's `at` signature with angle and lift parameters, and confirming surface scatter calls work with the bodyTube sweep. Then moving on to sketch out the tail base root sweep dimensions.

Now I'm sorting out fan layering order, colors, and quill placement — worried quills sitting flush in the same z-plane as the cards will z-fight since the cards are thin double-sided surfaces and the quill tubes have overlapping radius there.

Writing fan ring generation code...

Working through the remaining feather layers: layer D needs 21 fringe feathers spanning the full arc, supports E are a small set hidden behind the fan, and I'm now checking whether the covert layer F at z -0.30 would overlap the rump since that's close to the body's z -0.335.

Checking the covert sizing and ring radius more carefully, I confirm they clear the body geometry, then total up the tail joint count at 3 rings of 4 joints each. I'm adding a sweep for the tail quill base and double-checking the ring joints syntax before assembling the full structure.

Setting up imports and type helpers for the RGB palette and keyed interpolation function...

Adding more sweep configuration...

Adding lead ring sweeps around the neck joints with safety try/catch wraps, then planning a few more rings along the spine and starting to scatter scale cards across the body surface.

Refining the scatter filter so the scale cards land along the neck and front breast, restricting them by both depth and width so they don't spread onto the flanks where wing cards already sit.

I need to make sure the body mesh gets built before the scatter query runs against it, and I'm checking that all the card options—size, flow, lean, sink, vary, rng, cross, bone, bend—line up correctly for both the body scales and the wing cards, adjusting flow and lean values for the wing card placement.

Now I'm verifying the texture arrays, the glow function's typing against the mesh array, and the eye decal placement on the skull part. Writing the beak sweep geometry...

Setting the jaw joint position and aim direction, confirming the local axis convention for head coordinates. Now moving to write out the final textures for scale, crest tip, and eye details, aiming for consistent naming across roughly 600 lines. Starting the eye SVG markup...

I'm checking that the eye placement clears the crescent edges top and bottom so nothing overlaps awkwardly.

Setting the decal size ratio, then moving to defining the glass color palettes for each zone and verifying the ring-items typing flows correctly into the card frames. Now writing the wing card loop that builds frames along each row by interpolating body tube positions...

Checking the sign convention for left versus right wings and verifying the angle offsets place rows correctly between up and outward orientations, with the bone binding forcing attachment to the spine joint.

Now I'm mapping out the wing chain joints and finalizing colors like the quill's dark tone before writing the complete final answer carefully.
